# Introduction

Dates are one of the most common column types in real data and one of the easiest to get wrong.
They arrive split across several columns or as text in different formats. Months have different
lengths, and adding "one month" to January 31st has no obvious answer.

**lubridate** is the tidyverse package for dates and times. It is installed and attached with the
core `tidyverse` since version 2.0, so `library(tidyverse)` is all you need. This vignette walks
through the parts of lubridate you are most likely to use:

| Task | Functions |
|---|---|
| Build a date from parts or parse it from text | `make_date()`, `ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()` |
| Pull out components | `year()`, `month()`, `mday()`, `wday()`, `yday()` |
| Round dates down to a unit | `floor_date()` |
| Do arithmetic on dates | `days()`, `weeks()`, `months()`, `%m+%`, `days_in_month()` |
| Periods versus durations | `years()` versus `dyears()` |

Each function is shown on a toy example first, then used on a real dataset to answer a question.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
```

## The dataset

FiveThirtyEight published daily counts of US births from the Social Security Administration for
2000 through 2014, alongside its article
[*Some People Are Too Superstitious To Have A Baby On Friday The 13th*](https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/some-people-are-too-superstitious-to-have-a-baby-on-friday-the-13th/).
The file is public on FiveThirtyEight's GitHub, so it is read straight from the URL and nothing needs
downloading.

```{r}
#| label: load
births_raw <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/births/US_births_2000-2014_SSA.csv"
)

glimpse(births_raw)
```

There is one row per day, `r format(nrow(births_raw), big.mark = ",")` days in total. The date is
split over three numeric columns, and the weekday is a code from 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday). Neither
is a real date yet, so R cannot sort them by time, plot them on a time axis or do arithmetic on
them.

# Building and parsing dates

## `make_date()`: from separate columns

When the year, month and day sit in separate columns, `make_date()` combines them into a single
`Date`.

```{r}
#| label: make-date-toy
make_date(2014, 7, 4)
class(make_date(2014, 7, 4))
```

Applied to the dataset:

```{r}
#| label: make-date
births <- births_raw |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, month, date_of_month)) |>
  select(date, births, day_of_week)

head(births)
range(births$date)
```

## `ymd()` and friends: from text

When a date arrives as text, the parsing function is named after the **order** of its parts: `y`,
`m`, `d`. lubridate figures out the separators on its own, which is what makes these functions so
much easier than `as.Date()` with a format string.

```{r}
#| label: parse-text
ymd("2014-07-04")
ymd("20140704")
mdy("July 4, 2014")
mdy("07/04/2014")
dmy("04.07.2014")
```

All five return the same date. A string that does not match the order fails with a warning and
returns `NA`, rather than silently producing a wrong date:

```{r}
#| label: parse-fail
ymd("07/04/2014")
```

# Extracting components

Once a column is a real `Date`, one function call pulls out any component.

```{r}
#| label: extract-toy
d <- ymd("2014-07-04")

tibble(
  call   = c("year(d)", "month(d)", "month(d, label = TRUE)", "mday(d)",
             "wday(d, label = TRUE)", "yday(d)"),
  result = c(year(d), month(d), as.character(month(d, label = TRUE)), mday(d),
             as.character(wday(d, label = TRUE)), yday(d))
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

`label = TRUE` returns an **ordered factor** (`Jan < Feb < ...`), not a character string, so charts
and tables come out in calendar order rather than alphabetical order.

## A check worth making: `week_start`

`wday()` counts Sunday as day 1 by default, the US convention. This dataset counts Monday as day
1. Setting `week_start = 1` makes lubridate agree, which also gives a quick check that the dates
were built correctly:

```{r}
#| label: week-start
all(wday(births$date, week_start = 1) == births$day_of_week)
```

Every one of the `r format(nrow(births), big.mark = ",")` weekdays matches, so the supplied column
is no longer needed. From here on everything comes from `date` alone.

```{r}
#| label: add-components
births <- births |>
  select(date, births) |>
  mutate(
    year    = year(date),
    month   = month(date, label = TRUE),
    weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)
  )
```

## Question: which day of the week has the fewest births?

```{r}
#| label: weekday
overall_mean <- mean(births$births)

by_weekday <- births |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  summarise(avg_births = mean(births)) |>
  mutate(vs_average = avg_births / overall_mean - 1)

by_weekday |>
  mutate(avg_births = round(avg_births),
         vs_average = scales::percent(vs_average, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: weekday-plot
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(by_weekday, aes(weekday, avg_births)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_mean, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average births per day",
       title = "Far fewer babies are born on weekends",
       subtitle = "US, 2000-2014. Dashed line = overall daily average")
```

The effect is large. Sunday averages about a third fewer births than the typical day. Biology does
not work on a weekly schedule, but hospitals do: planned caesarean sections and inductions are
booked on weekdays. Because `weekday` is an ordered factor, the bars appear Monday to Sunday
without any extra sorting.

# Months have different lengths

A natural next question is which month has the most births. The obvious approach, summing births
by month, gives a misleading answer:

```{r}
#| label: month-total
births |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(total_births = sum(births)) |>
  arrange(total_births) |>
  head(3)
```

February comes out lowest mainly because it is shorter. `days_in_month()` returns the length of
the month a date falls in, and it accounts for leap years:

```{r}
#| label: dim-toy
days_in_month(ymd(c("2013-02-10", "2012-02-10", "2014-09-10")))
```

Dividing by the number of days gives a fair comparison. Equivalently, take the mean of the daily
counts:

```{r}
#| label: month-rate
by_month <- births |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(
    total_births   = sum(births),
    days           = n(),
    births_per_day = mean(births)
  )

by_month |>
  arrange(births_per_day) |>
  mutate(across(c(total_births, births_per_day), \(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ","))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Adjusted for length, February is no longer lowest. January is, and **September is highest**,
consistent with conceptions around the winter holidays. The two months are about 10% apart.

# Rounding dates with `floor_date()`

`floor_date()` rounds a date **down** to the start of a unit: week, month, quarter or year. It is
the standard way to aggregate daily data to a coarser time scale while keeping a real date that
plots correctly. (`ceiling_date()` and `round_date()` round up and to the nearest unit.)

```{r}
#| label: floor-toy
d <- ymd("2014-07-04")
floor_date(d, "week", week_start = 1)
floor_date(d, "month")
floor_date(d, "quarter")
floor_date(d, "year")
```

```{r}
#| label: floor-monthly
#| fig-height: 3.5
monthly <- births |>
  mutate(month_start = floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  group_by(month_start) |>
  summarise(births_per_day = mean(births))

ggplot(monthly, aes(month_start, births_per_day)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, span = 0.3, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average births per day",
       title = "Births peaked in 2007, then fell after the recession",
       subtitle = "Monthly averages, aggregated with floor_date(date, \"month\")")
```

Because `month_start` is still a `Date`, `scale_x_date()` can place breaks every two years and
format them with `date_labels`. If the grouping column had been built with `paste(year, month)`,
the axis would be text and both of those would be lost. The chart shows the seasonal wave
repeating each year on top of a trend that rose to 2007 and declined after the 2008 recession.

# Date arithmetic

## Periods: `days()`, `weeks()`, `months()`

Periods add calendar units to a date:

```{r}
#| label: period-toy
d <- ymd("2014-07-04")
d + days(1)
d - weeks(1)
d + months(2)
```

`weeks(1)` is the useful one in this dataset. The date exactly one week earlier or later falls on
the **same weekday**, which is how to compare a special day against normal days without the
weekend effect from section 3 getting in the way.

## The month-end trap and `%m+%`

Adding months is ambiguous at the end of a month. There is no February 31st, so lubridate returns
`NA` instead of guessing:

```{r}
#| label: month-trap
ymd("2014-01-31") + months(1)
```

The `%m+%` operator rolls back to the last valid day of the month instead, which is usually what a
billing date or a monthly report needs:

```{r}
#| label: month-safe
ymd("2014-01-31") %m+% months(1)
ymd("2014-01-31") %m+% months(1:3)
```

## Periods versus durations

lubridate has two kinds of time spans. A **period** (`years()`, `months()`, `days()`) follows the
calendar. A **duration** (`dyears()`, `ddays()`) is an exact number of seconds, and `dyears(1)` is
always 365.25 days. Across a leap year they disagree:

```{r}
#| label: period-duration
ymd("2012-01-01") + years(1)    # period: same calendar date next year
ymd("2012-01-01") + dyears(1)   # duration: 365.25 days later
```

2012 had 366 days, so adding 365.25 days stops short of New Year's Day, at 6 a.m. on December 31st.
The result is also a date-time rather than a date, because a duration counts seconds. For calendar
questions like "the same date next year", use periods. Use durations when you need
exact elapsed time, such as the length of an experiment.

## Question: do births drop on holidays?

To measure a holiday fairly, compare it with the same weekday one week before and one week after.
A small helper does this with `weeks(1)` and two joins:

```{r}
#| label: neighbour-fn
compare_to_neighbours <- function(days_of_interest) {
  lookup <- births |> select(date, births)

  days_of_interest |>
    select(date, births) |>
    mutate(week_before = date - weeks(1),
           week_after  = date + weeks(1)) |>
    left_join(lookup |> rename(births_before = births), by = c("week_before" = "date")) |>
    left_join(lookup |> rename(births_after  = births), by = c("week_after"  = "date")) |>
    # At the edges of the data (e.g. 1 Jan 2000) one neighbour is missing; use the other
    mutate(reference = rowMeans(cbind(births_before, births_after), na.rm = TRUE),
           vs_neighbours = births / reference - 1)
}
```

Holidays are selected with `month()` and `mday()`, so no list of 15 separate dates is needed.

```{r}
#| label: holidays
holidays <- tribble(
  ~holiday,           ~m, ~d,
  "New Year's Day",    1,  1,
  "Valentine's Day",   2, 14,
  "Independence Day",  7,  4,
  "Halloween",        10, 31,
  "Christmas Eve",    12, 24,
  "Christmas Day",    12, 25
)

holiday_effect <- holidays |>
  mutate(result = map2(m, d, \(m, d) {
    births |>
      filter(month(date) == m, mday(date) == d) |>
      compare_to_neighbours() |>
      summarise(years = n(), avg_change = mean(vs_neighbours))
  })) |>
  unnest(result) |>
  arrange(avg_change)

holiday_effect |>
  transmute(holiday, years, avg_change = scales::percent(avg_change, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Christmas Day has about a third fewer births than the same weekday a week either side, and
Independence Day a quarter fewer. The pattern is the same as the weekend effect: scheduled
deliveries are moved away from days when staff are off. Valentine's Day is the only date here
with *more* births than its neighbours.

## Question: is Friday the 13th avoided?

This is the question from the FiveThirtyEight article. Every 13th of the month is compared with the
6th and the 20th, which are exactly one week either side and so fall on the same weekday. The
results are then grouped by the weekday of the 13th, so Friday can be compared with the other days.

```{r}
#| label: friday-13
thirteenths <- births |>
  filter(mday(date) == 13) |>
  compare_to_neighbours() |>
  mutate(weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1))

by_weekday_13 <- thirteenths |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  summarise(occurrences = n(), avg_change = mean(vs_neighbours))

by_weekday_13 |>
  mutate(avg_change = scales::percent(avg_change, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: friday-13-plot
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(by_weekday_13, aes(weekday, avg_change, fill = weekday == "Fri")) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "firebrick", `FALSE` = "grey65"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Weekday of the 13th", y = "Births vs. same weekday ±1 week",
       title = "Friday the 13th has noticeably fewer births",
       subtitle = "US, 2000-2014, each 13th compared with the 6th and 20th of the same month")
```

Every 13th has slightly fewer births than its neighbours, about 1-4% depending on the weekday.
Friday the 13th stands out at roughly **6% fewer**, nearly double the next-lowest weekday (Thursday, about 3.6%). With 25
Friday the 13ths in the data, the gap is consistent with the article's conclusion that some
scheduled births are moved away from the date.

# Summary

| Function | What it does | Used here to |
|---|---|---|
| `make_date()` | Build a `Date` from year, month, day columns | Combine the three date columns |
| `ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()` | Parse text in a given order | Parse five formats of the same date |
| `wday(label = TRUE, week_start = 1)` | Weekday as an ordered factor | Verify the data; weekday effect |
| `month()`, `mday()`, `year()` | Extract a component | Group by month; select holidays and 13ths |
| `days_in_month()` | Length of the month, leap-aware | Show why monthly totals mislead |
| `floor_date()` | Round down to a unit | Aggregate days to months for a time series |
| `weeks()`, `days()`, `months()` | Calendar periods | Find the same weekday a week away |
| `%m+%` | Add months without producing `NA` | Handle month-end dates |
| `years()` vs `dyears()` | Period vs exact duration | Show the leap-year difference |

Three habits from this vignette carry over to any dataset with dates:

1. **Convert to a real `Date` first.** Everything after that, including sorting, plotting,
   rounding and arithmetic, depends on it.
2. **Compare like with like.** Months of different lengths and days with different weekdays
   produce misleading totals. Here `days_in_month()` and `weeks(1)` fixed that.
3. **Use `label = TRUE`.** Ordered factors keep tables and charts in calendar order without extra
   sorting.
